发布源: Bruegel --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

Reading time: 28 minutes

Reading time: 28 minutes

Executive summary

The European Central Bank faces substantial change in its decision-making structures. Most of its six-strong leadership team on the Executive Board is due to be replaced within a relatively limited period around President Christine Lagarde’s departure in February 2027. This offers an opportunity to take stock and make institutional improvements.

The ECB’s responsibilities have grown substantially over time and now span a wide range of duties, from traditional monetary policy to banking supervision, payments technology and international economic governance. The Executive Board needs diversity of expertise: skill considerations should play a bigger role in its inherently political appointment processes. Preventing bunching of appointments, in line with the original 1998 design of staggered board terms, could also help maintain continuity.

Structured strategy reviews could take place as part of the handover from one ECB President to another, facilitating strategic reflection. The Governing Council also could adjust how it handles policy announcements, quiet periods, contrasting views and meeting summaries to help with policy transmission.

item.content:encoded:
How can Europe turn higher defence spending into greater military capability?

发布源: Bruegel --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

Europe’s spending on defence equipment is set tomore than doublebetween 2022 and 2026, but its procurement market remains fragmented. Recent data shows that only24%of European Union defence equipment procurement was collaborative, well below the 35% benchmark. National preferences for bespoke models keep orders small and competitionweak, andgive firms little reason to expand production.

Several initiatives tackle different parts of this problem: the EU’s SAFE programme offers cheaper loans for joint purchases; NATO works to match demand with industrial capacity; and the proposed Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) and Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) would add more multilateral finance. No initiative yet combineslarge pooledorders with a binding commitment to open contracts to partners’ firms, meaning that more spending is unlikely to strengthen competition.

An expanded MDM could address this gap. Starting with countries whose military requirements already overlap, the MDM could turn agreement on individual capabilities into a funded, multi-year procurement programme. Governments would agree common requirements first, then let suppliers from all participating countries compete. This would offer multiple benefits: countries with high borrowing costs would get access to cheaper finance, while others could be attracted by shared stocks, a larger supplier pool and faster delivery. item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Bruegel --Belgium官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
More flexible European Union spending needs stronger parliamentary scrutiny

发布源: Bruegel --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) gives the European Parliament significant powers in relation to the European Union’s budget. The EU’s overall seven-year budget – the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – cannot pass without the parliament’s consent, while the parliament acts as co-legislator alongside the Council of the EU in the annual budgetary procedure1. Together with the Council, the parliament thus has the authority to determine how EU funds are allocated.

However, the European Commission’s proposal for the 2028-2034 MFF foresees a new architecture for the EU budget, which would exclude the European Parliament from significant allocation decisions and limit its scrutiny powers during implementation2. This is problematic not only from a treaty perspective, but also because the parliament, as the EU’s democratically elected institution, should help ensure that EU spending serves EU priorities.

The Commission’s proposals would give national governments a greater role in allocating EU funds across priorities. Governments may be tempted to use these funds to pursue domestic objectives, which might not necessarily coincide with European priorities. Given that the EU budget accounts for little more than one percent of GDP, compared with public expenditure of around 45 percent of GDP at national level, it is essential that EU spending remains focused on common European priorities.

item.content:encoded:
Global Order and Peacemaking

发布源: International Crisis Group (ICG) --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

The framework of international law, multilateral institutions and major-power cooperation that shaped post-Cold War peacemaking has broken down. The Global Order and Peacemaking Project explores the new landscape for conflict prevention and resolution, linking Crisis Group’s research on individual countries and regions to shifts in international affairs. Through our analysis and advocacy, we aim to influence debates on trends in conflict, propose new approaches to peacemaking and identify new ways for states to reduce risks of war.

With the post-World War II international order fading away and hostilities on the rise, the prospects for conflict prevention look dim. But the picture is not wholly dark. It is possible to identify tools that, if used properly, can reduce bloodshed.

Oil, gas and fuel prices are central to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, with Washington striving to lower them and Tehran to keep them high. With both sides determined to prevail, five market-shaping developments in particular could affect whether fighting ramps up or de-escalates.

From Early Warning to Early Action

发布源: International Crisis Group (ICG) --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

Ringing the alarm bell has been at the core of Crisis Group’s mission since its inception in 1995. We have called for action to prevent deadly violence, mass atrocities and political destabilisation. Through a range of tools and publications – includingCrisisWatchour monthly global conflict tracker – and targeted engagement at the local, regional and global levels, we strive to alert the policy community on upcoming risks and potential opportunities for conflict resolution in some 70 conflicts, crises and vulnerable countries.

Read the CrisisWatch 20th anniversary brochurehere.

This edition of On the Horizon includes entries on Chad, Cuba, food insecurity in the Horn of Africa and Pakistan, sounding the alarm about conflicts and crises that may emerge or escalate in the next three to six months. It identifies key actors and dates to watch in support of global conflict prevention efforts.

Friends of the EPC Fund

发布源: European Policy Centre (EPC) --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

A new Friends of EPC Fund has been launched, which will allow individuals and organisations to donate to a portfolio of projects that support the general strategic objectives of the EPC.It will contribute to the EPC’s funding diversity, allowing a broader base of individuals and organisations to support our work. The new fund is a contribution to securing the long-term financial future of the EPC, providing a hands-off way to support the EPC, fully respecting its independence and intellectual autonomy. The ’Friends of’ funds are hosted by the King Baudouin Foundation.By creating a ‘Friends of’ fund, a group of philanthropists decides to support a particular organisation or association in a structural and sustainable way.

Donations by organisations and individuals may be made by electronic transfer, credit card, or QR code. The King Baudouin Foundation can provide tax certificates for donations over €40 under conditions set out on the KBF Website.It is one of a series of “Friends of…” funds at the King Baudouin Foundation that allow organisations to raise funds.More information on the “Friends of…” concept and detailed information on donation conditions is available athttps://donate.kbs-frb.be/actions/FFO-EuropeanPolicyCentre

item.content:encoded:
From Sovereignty to Managed Interdependence: A Forward-Looking Agenda for EU Qua...

发布源: European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

Quantum technologies are increasingly becoming part of technology sovereignty debates, as governments seek greater control over critical capabilities linked to national security, economic competitiveness, and strategic autonomy. However, the emerging policy debate, in Europe and elsewhere, risks framing sovereignty too narrowly – as a means of achieving self-sufficiency across the entire quantum computing stack. Such an approach is unlikely to deliver the outcomes policymakers seek. Instead, Europe should pursue amodel ofmanaged interdependence: reserving direct control for the narrow set of dependencies that pose genuine and severe strategic risks, while strengthening the international connections, partnerships, and capabilities that allow European ecosystems to innovate, commercialise, and benefit from quantum computing.

The sector is particularly important because of its potential applications across areas including drug discovery, materials science, chemistry, cryptography, and defence-related use cases. At the same time, quantum computing is expected to create economic value primarily through adoption and diffusion across the wider economy rather than through direct ownership of quantum hardware by most firms. The central economic objective is therefore not simply to build European quantum companies, but to ensure that European industries can access, adopt, and benefit from quantum capabilities.

item.content:encoded:
Changing South Caucasus: Time for EU Leadership

发布源: European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

By Ambassador Teimuraz Janjalia, Senior Fellow, EU Awareness Centre

The South Caucasus is a strategic crossroad of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, and its geopolitical significance has grown markedly in the past six years. The development is driven by regional and systemic shocks such as the 2020 Karabakh war, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the rapid reconfiguration of transit and energy corridors, most notably the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor. At the same time, regional powers such as Turkey, China, and Iran have become more assertive, and the United States is clearly renewing its strategy for the region. These transformations elevate the region’s importance for Europe and its ambitions for connectivity, supply-chain resilience, and energy diversification. They introduce complex challenges but also present opportunities for the European Union’s traditional framework of engagement.

Currently, the European Union has a broad and diverse range of instruments and institutional frameworks for regional interaction. These mechanisms encompass bilateral relationships with Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia, the long-standing multilateral architecture of the Eastern Partnership, the high-leverage Global Gateway Strategy with its connectivity platform, and the recently prioritised Black Sea Strategy. CitiesTake the Lead on Climate ActionThere is no secure and competitive Europe without sustainability. As European cities take the centre stage of this transition, the real challenge lies in delivering it under real economic and political constraints. To explore the path ahead, the Lisbon Council convened the2026 Sustainable Cities Summit on ‘Squaring the Green Circle: Climate Action, Economic Urgency, Urban Reality.’The summit served to launch theSustainable Cities Lab,a new initiative to move fromwhatmust be done tohowEurope delivers.

发布源: Lisbon Council for Economic Competitiveness and Social Renewal --Belgium | 抓取时间: 2026-11-04

There is no secure and competitive Europe without sustainability. And European cities now sit at the centre of the green transition: they are the primary markets for clean industry and the places where high-level European Union targets must be reconciled with the daily realities of housing, energy and mobility. While around 70% of European Union legislation is implemented at the local level, a persistent gap remains between climate ambition and actual delivery. To explore how to bridge this gap and turn policy into practice, the Lisbon Council convened the2026 Sustainable Cities Summit on ‘Squaring the Green Circle: Climate Action, Economic Urgency, Urban Reality,’bringing together leading policymakers, city practitioners, investors and urban innovators.

The summit opened with aHigh-Level Roundtable on ‘Scaling Sustainability in a Tougher Climate: What Europe’s Cities Have Learned and What Comes Next,’a candid, peer-to-peer exchange between senior city leaders and experts. From the lived experience of key cities, includingBrussels, Cluj-Napoca, Copenhagen, Firenze, Ferrara, Hamburg, Leuven, Madrid and Riga,the discussion highlighted what can realistically be replicated and scaled across diverse urban contexts.
